output.methodChoice: Collected X1 (scan timings and write-off rates by receiving shift) first, to test the DC-handling explanation directly with the unchanged day shift as a comparison. Then collected X11 (independent trailer telematics) to test the Haverlow-temperature claim. Stopped at two items.
output.brief:
Most of the jump is spoilage inside Brackenford, not Haverlow's fault. About £15,700 of the £18,400 weekly rise is DC-stage write-offs. Since the 27 July Phase 2 cut (night receiving six to four), night chilled pallets wait a median 3 h 52 min to reach a chamber (was 44 min) on an unrefrigerated dock averaging 15–17°C. Night write-offs rose from 0.6% to 2.9% of lots; the day shift stayed flat. Trailer telematics show Haverlow product at 2.4–3.5°C when doors opened; the 6.6–7.9°C probe readings were keyed about 3.5 hours after unloading finished. Pellridge and own-label night lots spoil at the same rate; their day lots are normal. Chambers are fine.

Next: withdraw the Haverlow chargeback and drop the volume move; restore six night operatives (its £2,300/week saving is far smaller than the losses) and set a maximum dock-to-chamber time, tracked weekly from scan data. Keep the night probe.

Credits (about £2,700 of the rise): Corriebank's looser claim rules may explain some, but it's unproven; other customers' credits also rose. Get Corriebank's claim-level data and check a sample against lots and shifts before changing terms.

Confidence: about 90% on the dock cause; moderate on credits.
